Martial arts movies live or die by the fight. Even the greatest American-made martial arts movies owe a huge debt to performers and filmmakers who turned fight choreography into an art form.

Ip Man (2008) — Ip Man Vs. 10 Black Belts

Donnie Yen's Ip Man spends much of the 2008 movie displaying remarkable restraint. That disappears after the death of his friend, when the Wing Chun master enters a Japanese dojo and asks to fight 10 karate black belts at once.

blocks.x: The scene lasts only a few minutes, but Yen's change in demeanor makes every strike feel angrier than the last. The Legend Of Drunken Master (1994) — Wong Fei-Hung's Final Fight
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/instar49594449.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

Jackie Chan was already one of the world's greatest martial arts performers when Drunken Master II, later released in the U.S. as The Legend of Drunken Master, arrived in 1994. Its climactic battle against Ken Lo demonstrates exactly what decades of experience, extraordinary athletic ability, and fearless physical comedy could produce.

Lo's kicking ability gives the fight astonishing speed, while Chan's drunken boxing turns imbalance into a weapon. Wong Fei-hung bends, falls, twists, and attacks from positions that look physically impossible. The industrial setting adds fire and hot coals to an already complicated piece of choreography. Few fights combine comedy and genuine physical danger without allowing one to undermine the other.

3
Police Story (1985) — The Shopping Mall Fight
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/07/screen-hub-cast-placeholder-1.png?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

Jackie Chan's Police Story contains enough dangerous stunts for several action movies, but everything comes together during its enormous shopping mall finale. Chan fights through henchmen while motorcycles, railings, display cases, and an alarming amount of glass become part of the choreography.

The environment is why the sequence ranks above more technically pure one-on-one fights. Chan never treats the set as background. Almost everything can become a weapon, obstacle, or something for a stunt performer to crash through. The famous pole slide provides the exclamation point, but the entire sequence represents Chan's approach to action filmmaking at its most fearless.
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/amazon01_logo-1.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

2
The Way Of The Dragon (1972) — Tang Lung Vs. Colt

Bruce Lee versus Chuck Norris sounds almost too perfectly designed to become martial arts history. The Way of the Dragon saves the encounter for Rome's Colosseum, where Lee's Tang Lung faces Norris' Colt in a fight that feels unusually patient compared with many modern action sequences.

The two men study each other before the rhythm begins to change. Colt initially has the advantage, forcing Tang Lung to loosen his movement and adapt. Lee's influence extended far beyond his own films, inspiring generations of martial arts movies that followed in his footsteps. More than 50 years later, two martial arts icons silently circling each other inside the Colosseum remains difficult to beat.

1
The Raid 2 (2014) — Rama Vs. The Assassin

The Raid had already changed expectations for modern martial arts action, yet Gareth Evans somehow raised them with The Raid 2. The sequel contains multiple contenders for this ranking, but Rama's kitchen battle against Cecep Arif Rahman's Assassin is the sequence everything has been building toward.

There is almost nothing to distract from Iko Uwais and Rahman. The white kitchen gives the camera room to capture every movement as an already brutal hand-to-hand fight gradually introduces knives. Neither performer appears invincible. They become exhausted, injured, increasingly desperate, and more dangerous as the fight continues.

The sequence also makes especially clever use of the Assassin's kerambit blades, a detail that gives The Raid 2's final martial arts fight another layer of danger. What ultimately puts it at No. 1, however, is how completely everything works together.

The choreography changes as the opponents learn each other, and the violence becomes more frightening precisely because viewers can follow what is happening. There are bigger martial arts sequences and more historically important ones, but few combine physical performance, choreography, camerawork, and escalating danger this completely. For several minutes, The Raid 2 shows just how good a movie fight can possibly be.

The Raid 2 is a 2014 Indonesian action thriller that continues Rama’s story shortly after The Raid, sending the elite police officer undercover inside Jakarta’s criminal underworld to expose corruption within his own department.
